prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you type an HTTPS address into a browser and press enter, the browser first has to work out what you actually asked for. It parses the address into a scheme, a hostname, an optional port, a path, and a query string, and it fills in defaults where they are missing, so https implies port 443. Before touching the network, the browser checks its own state. It may find a cached copy of the resource that is still fresh, and in that case it can skip the network entirely. It also consults its HSTS list, which tells it that certain sites must only ever be contacted over HTTPS, and it may look for an existing open connection to the same server that it can reuse.

If nothing local answers the request, the browser needs an IP address, because networks route packets by number and not by name. This is the job of the Domain Name System. The browser looks in its own DNS cache first, then asks the operating system, which keeps a cache of its own and may consult the hosts file. If neither knows the answer, the request goes to a recursive resolver, usually run by your internet provider or a public service. That resolver either answers from its cache or works down the hierarchy, asking a root server which servers handle the top-level domain, asking those which servers are authoritative for the domain, and finally asking the authoritative server for the address. Each answer carries a time-to-live that says how long it may be cached, which is why a DNS change can take a while to be seen everywhere. Modern browsers may also ask for HTTPS records that advertise supported protocols, and some send the query over an encrypted channel.

With an IP address in hand, the browser opens a connection. Classic HTTPS runs over TCP, which begins with a three-step handshake. The client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with a SYN-ACK, and the client answers with an ACK. This costs one full round trip before any useful data can flow, so the physical distance to the server matters directly here. Increasingly, sites use HTTP/3 instead, which runs over QUIC on top of UDP and folds the transport setup and the encryption setup into a single exchange. Whichever transport is used, the packets travel through your router, your provider's network, and a series of other networks, each of which forwards them one hop closer to the destination.

Next comes the TLS handshake, which is what makes the connection secure. In TLS 1.3, the client opens with a hello message that lists the encryption algorithms it supports, includes a key share for a Diffie-Hellman style exchange, and names the host it wants through the Server Name Indication extension. That extension matters because one IP address can serve many sites, and the server needs to know which certificate to present. The server replies with its own key share, which lets both sides derive the same session keys without ever sending those keys over the wire. The server also sends its certificate and a signature proving it holds the matching private key. From that point on, everything is encrypted.

The browser then validates the certificate, and this is the step that gives HTTPS its meaning. It checks that the certificate covers the requested hostname, that it has not expired, and that it chains up through one or more intermediate certificates to a certificate authority your operating system or browser already trusts. It may also check whether the certificate has been revoked, using stapled OCSP responses or compact revocation lists. If any of these checks fail, the browser stops and shows a warning page, and no request is sent. If they pass, the client confirms it has derived the keys, and the connection is ready. TLS 1.3 needs only one round trip for all of this, and a returning visitor can sometimes resume a previous session and send data immediately, although that shortcut carries some replay-related caveats.

Only now does the browser actually send its HTTP request, and in a sense this is the real beginning of the exchange rather than its end. The request consists of a method such as GET, the path, and a set of headers. These include the Host or authority, the browser's accepted content encodings, its language preferences, and any cookies stored for that site. With HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 these headers are compressed, and many requests can share one connection at the same time. Everything is encrypted by TLS before it leaves your machine, so intermediaries along the way can see roughly how much data moved and who the server is, but not what was said.

The request now crosses the network again and arrives at the destination, which is rarely a single machine. It typically reaches a CDN edge node or a load balancer, which may terminate TLS itself, serve a cached response if it has one, or choose a backend server to forward the request to. The backend application may check authentication, query a database, call other internal services, and render a page, all of which take time. The delay between sending the request and receiving the first byte of the answer is known as time to first byte, and it combines everything described so far: DNS lookup, connection setup, the TLS handshake, network latency in both directions, and the server's own processing time.

When the server is ready, it sends back a status line and response headers, followed by the start of the body. The first byte of that response, arriving through the encrypted connection and being decrypted by the browser, is the moment this whole sequence ends. Everything afterward, such as parsing the HTML, discovering stylesheets and scripts, and fetching more resources, is a separate process that begins with that first byte. For a developer, the practical lesson is that a slow first byte can come from many places, so it helps to measure each stage separately in the browser's network panel before deciding what to optimize.
